senses.gloss:
āgamas
(‘sacred books which teach the Truth from all aspects’)
------------------------------------------
Āgamas are a certain class of Hindu religious literature which practically form the basis of Hindu religious practices of the post-Vedic era. Literally, the word means ‘that which teaches Truth from all aspects,’ ā samantāt gamayati, and hence can denote the वेदस्, or for that matter, any sacred book. But in practice it is used in a more restricted sense to indicate the above-mentioned class of literature.
Though the आगमस् are definitely post-Vedic since they deal elaborately with the deities शिव, शक्ति and विष्णु, their temples and rituals, it is rather difficult to fix their chronological origin and development. It can be definitely stated that some of the आगमस् devoted to the cult of विष्णु were already in existence by the time of the Mahābhārata. The development of various आगमस् might have continued till the 8th cent. A. D.
A typical āgama is generally divided into four parts known as ‘pādas.’ In the Vidyāpāda or Jñānapāda philosophical and metaphysical subjects are discussed. In the Yogapāda details of yogic practices required to purify the body and मिन्द् are given. In the Kriyāpāda, which is usually voluminous, temple architecture and इचोनोग्रफ्य् are dealt with. In the Caryāpāda, the details of spiritual sacraments as also the code of conduct expected of a novice are delineated.
According to the deity propitiated, the आगमस् are divided into three broad groups: शैवागमस्, शाक्तागमस् and Vaiṣṇavāgamas. The twenty eight आगमस् starting with Kāmikāgama and ending with Vātulāgama comprise the Śaivā-gamas. According to them, शिव the Supreme God is ‘pati’ (the Lord), the jīvas or individual souls are ‘paśu’ (animal in bondage) and the three kinds of malas or impurities (āṇavamala, kārmikamala and māyāmala) comprise the ‘pāśa’ (rope) by which the jīvas are bound. It is by the grace of शिव, the पशुपति, that the paśus are able to get rid of their pāśas and get मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन्.
The शाक्तागमस्, also known as तन्त्रस्, are legion in number. They follow the शैवागमस् very closely, the only exception being that शक्ति or देवी (Power or consort of शिव) gets the supreme place. The tāntric discipline has become divided into दक्षिणाचार (the right-hand path), also known as ‘samaya,’ and वामाचार (the left-hand path), also called ‘kaula.’ The former conforms to the decent and accepted norms of spiritual practice whereas the latter seems to advocate the theory that even aberrations can be sublimated to the level of the spiritual practice resulting in the experience of the same supreme Truth.
The Vaiṣṇavāgamas, also called Saṁhitās, are divided into the Vaikhānasa and the Pāñcarātra schools. Both teach that विष्णु is the highest Truth and stress the importance of worship in temples.
Jainism also has its आगमस् written in the Ardhamāgadhi language, and is divided into two: Śrutāṅgas and Upāṅgas.
See also DAKṢIṆĀCĀRA, KAULA-MĀRGA, PĀÑCARĀTRĀGAMAS, ŚAIVĀGAMAS, ŚĀKTĀ-GAMAS, SAMAYAMATA, TANTRAS, VAIKHĀ-NASĀGAMA and VĀMĀCĀRA.

Āgamanī
(‘welcome’ [songs])
------------------------------------------
Śrī दुर्गापूजा is one of the major festivals of the Hindus celebrated on a grand scale in Bengal, Orissa, Bihar and Assam. Beautiful clay images are ceremonially installed during the period of nine days (1st to 9th in the month of Āśvina, śuklapakṣa or bright half) (October) and elaborate worship performed. ‘Āgamanī’ is the name given to a particular type of songs generally sung on this occasion as part of the ‘Kālīkīrtan’ programmes.
Śrī दुर्गा is actually पार्वती or Umā, the beloved daughter of queen Menā and king Girirāja (the king of हिमालयस्), given in मर्रिअगे to Lord शिव. It is long since the daughter has visited the होउसे of her parents. The parents, especially the मोथेर् Menā, are anxious about her welfare since rumours have reached their ears that their daughter is languishing in her husband’s होउसे owing to his poverty and queer ways of life. The आगमनी songs depict their concern and anxiety for their daughter and anger towards their son-in-law. They are full of tenderness of the मोथेर्’s love for the daughter. Solicitude for the welfare of Umā, disgust with शिव’s way of life—especially his living in the च्रेमतिओन् grounds, besmearing his body with ashes and begging his food—consequent anger expressing itself in a resolve not to send her back to her husband’s होउसे and even a grim determination to fight a wordy duel with him if he presses for her return—these are some of the sentiments frequently found in these songs. Rāmprasād, Kamalākānta and Dāśarathi are some of the well-known mystic poets who have composed these songs.

āgāmī-karma
(‘the future कर्म’)
------------------------------------------
Belief in कर्म and पुनर्जन्म (reincarnation) is one of the fundamental dogmas of हिन्दुइस्म्, जैनिस्म्, बुद्धिस्म् and सिखिस्म्. कर्म or action, good or bad, must have its effect. आगामी-कर्म is the कर्म that is being done now or that will be done in future (before death) which will produce its results later.
For details see KARMA.

Agastya
(‘One who stunted the growth of the mountain विन्ध्य’)
------------------------------------------
Agastya is one of the most famous ṛṣis (sages or seers) frequently met with in Hindu religious lore. He is the seer of several Ṛgvedic mantras (Ṛgveda Saṁhitā 1.166 to 191). He is a ब्रह्मर्षि, the son of पुलस्त्य and Havirbhuk. Sage Agniveśya is his disciple.
According to another version he was the son of मित्र and वरुण, and was born in a kumbha or jar. Hence the names Kumbhaja, Kumbhodbhava, Kalaśīsuta and so on. वसिष्ठ was his brother. He married लोपामुद्रा (also known as कावेरी), the princess of Vidarbha and begot a son Dṛḍhāsya, also known as इध्मवाह. A man of vast knowledge and severe austerity he is said to have destroyed the demons इल्वल and वातापि, stunted the growth of the विन्ध्य mountain which was growing recklessly, obstructing the light of the sun, drunk the waters of the ocean to expose the demons Kālakeyas who were killed by the gods, to have been honoured by राम when he was living in the दण्डकारण्य and to whom he gave divine weapons and also taught the Ādityahṛdaya-hymn later and brought about reconciliation between इन्द्र and the Maruts.
Though अगस्त्य is not enumerated among the सप्तर्षिस् (the seven great sages), he is included among the progenitors of ‘gotra’ geneology. He has been accorded a stellar status and identified with Canopus, the brightest star in the sky of southern India.
In the annals of Tamil religious lore and literature, अगस्त्य is the accredited originator of the Tamil language, the author of the maiden grammar of that language and the first president of the first organization of Tamil litterateurs. He is also credited with the authorship of several works on medicine, म्य्स्तिचिस्म् and magic. One work called Agastya Saṁhitā which deals with ritualistic worship is available. It is part of Pāñcarātra literature. He is said to have visited several South East Asian countries like Borneo, Siam and Cambodia.
The word ‘Agastya’ might have been a title. Several Agastyas may have been involved in these stories, syncretised into one.
An Agastyāśrama, a hermitage of अगस्त्य, has been mentioned in the Rāmāyaṇa. This has been sometimes identified with Agastyapurī, east of Nasik in Maharashtra state.
The Vanaparva of Mahābhārata (88.13) mentions an Agastyatīrtha in the Pāṇḍya country as an important place of पिल्ग्रिमगे.
Seeing the star अगस्त्य or Canopus when the sun is in the middle of कन्या or Virgo and worshipping him at night is mentioned as a vrata (religious rite).
See also ĀDITYAHṚDAYA, GOTRA and LOPĀMUDRĀ.
